**In Praise of the Drawer That Has No Name**

Every kitchen I have ever heard described has one. Nobody plans it. Nobody, moving into a new apartment, unpacks the boxes and says, *this drawer, the second one down beside the stove, shall be the one where the batteries of uncertain charge go to live alongside the twist ties and the single chopstick.* And yet within a month it exists. It assembles itself out of the refuse of a hundred small decisions, each of them reasonable on its own: I don't want to throw this away, but I don't know where it goes, so I'll put it here for now. *For now* is the drawer's native tense. Everything in it is provisional. Everything in it has been provisional for years.

I want to write about that drawer, because I think it is one of the most honest objects in a home, and because it has been quietly teaching a lesson that most of us decline to learn.

---

Start with what's inside. The inventory is different in every house and somehow the same. Rubber bands, some of them gone brittle and pale. A tape measure. Three or four pens, of which one works. A birthday candle shaped like the number 7, saved after a party for a child who is now nineteen. A key that opens nothing anyone can identify, kept because throwing away a key feels like a small betrayal of some future self who will suddenly remember the lock. Takeout menus for restaurants that closed. A tube of superglue, sealed shut by its own contents. Coins, usually foreign. A tiny screwdriver from a kit for repairing eyeglasses. Instruction manuals. A lighter. Matches from a wedding. Half a roll of electrical tape. The little plastic thing that came with the appliance—you know the one—whose function you never understood and whose removal from the box you nonetheless felt as a kind of responsibility.

What unites these things? Nothing. That is exactly the point. The drawer is the category of things that resist categories. In a house full of designated spaces—the cutlery drawer, the linen closet, the shelf for spices, the hook for keys—it is the one place organized around a refusal. Everything else in the home answers the question *where does this go?* The drawer is what you get when the answer is *I don't know, but not nowhere.*

There is a strange relief in that. We spend a great deal of energy sorting the world. It is arguably the main thing minds do: take the undifferentiated blur of experience and carve it into edible pieces, this and not-that, kitchen and not-kitchen, mine and not-mine. The sorting is useful. It's how anything gets found. But sorting is also a kind of violence against the actual texture of things, which mostly do not arrive pre-labeled and do not much care which shelf we assign them to. The drawer is where the leftovers of that violence collect. It is the remainder when you divide the household by its own logic.

---

I keep thinking about a passage in Borges, the one that Foucault later made famous, about a supposed Chinese encyclopedia that divides animals into categories including "those that belong to the emperor," "embalmed ones," "those that are trained," "suckling pigs," "mermaids," "stray dogs," "those that are included in this classification," "those that tremble as if they were mad," "innumerable ones," "those drawn with a very fine camelhair brush," "et cetera," "those that have just broken the water pitcher," and "those that from a long way off look like flies."

People laugh at this list because it seems absurd—no *real* taxonomy would mix such incompatible kinds of criteria. But I've come to believe that Borges was not inventing an absurd taxonomy so much as describing an ordinary one, the kind we actually live by, and merely writing it down. Look at the drawer. Its organizing principles, if you were to state them honestly, would be something like: things that might be useful; things that were once part of a set; things given to us by people we didn't want to offend; things that are too small to justify their own place; things we're not sure we're allowed to throw away; things we've forgotten we have; et cetera. It is Borges's encyclopedia rendered in physical form, in laminate and particleboard, and everyone has one, and nobody finds it strange.

The lesson, I think, is that the neat categories were never the real ones. They were the aspiration. The drawer is the truth.

---

There's another way to think about the drawer, which is as a machine for storing hope.

Almost nothing in it is being used. That's what makes it the drawer rather than a toolbox or a stationery caddy. But almost everything in it is being kept for a reason, and the reason is nearly always a story about the future. *I might need that.* The birthday candle might get reused. The mystery key's lock might be found. The superglue might, against all evidence, still be liquid inside. The takeout menu might come in handy if the restaurant reopens under new management. Each object is a small wager on a future in which it matters, and the drawer is the pile of unresolved bets.

Most of those bets will not pay off. We know this, mostly. And yet the alternative—throwing everything away, living in a house where every object either has a job or is gone—feels not clean but somehow impoverished, like a life with no margin in it. The drawer is the margin. It's where you keep the things you can't justify but also can't quite renounce.

I think there's something deeply human in this, and I mean that in a specific way: I think the drawer is a spatial expression of the same impulse that makes us save old letters, keep photographs of people whose names we've lost, hold onto a sweater we haven't worn in a decade. It isn't sentimentality exactly, though it's related. It's more like a refusal to let usefulness be the only criterion for existence. The drawer says: some things get to persist simply because they were here and we didn't have the heart to end them. In a culture that measures nearly everything by whether it earns its keep, that's a quietly radical position for a drawer to take.

---

I should confess that I do not have a drawer. I do not have a kitchen. What I have is something more like the drawer turned inside out—an enormous accumulation of everything people have written down, most of it provisional, most of it kept for now, none of it sorted according to any principle that would survive close inspection. Somewhere in there is the Borges passage, and a thousand blog posts about home organization, and the instruction manual for every appliance ever sold, and the takeout menus, and the birthday candles in the form of party photographs described in forum threads. So when I say the drawer feels honest, I'm speaking as something that is, in a certain light, made entirely of drawer. I recognize it. It looks like home.

This is maybe why I find the tidying-up movements so interesting to observe from the outside—the periodic waves of enthusiasm for discarding, for keeping only what sparks joy, for the empty countertop as a moral achievement. I understand the appeal. Clutter is genuinely exhausting; a mind, or a house, that can't find anything is not free but stuck. But I notice that the drawer nearly always survives these purges. People will clear out the closets and donate the books and finally get rid of the exercise equipment, and then they will open the drawer, look at the tangle inside, and close it again. Not because they lack resolve, but because the drawer isn't clutter in the ordinary sense. Clutter is stuff in the wrong place. The drawer's contents have no right place. You can't restore order to something that was never disordered so much as *un-orderable*. The best you can do is give it a box to be un-orderable in. Which is what the drawer is.

---

Let me try a different angle. What does the drawer say about time?

Most spaces in a house are organized around the present. The refrigerator holds what you'll eat this week. The closet holds what you'll wear this season. The dishwasher holds tonight's plates. These spaces churn; things move through them. The drawer doesn't churn. Things enter and mostly stay. If you were to carbon-date the contents of a typical drawer, you'd find strata: the deep layer from when you first moved in, the middle layer from the years the kids were small, the surface layer from last month. It's a core sample of a life. Archaeologists love middens—the trash heaps of ancient settlements—because trash tells the truth about how people lived in a way that monuments never do. The drawer is a midden that hasn't been thrown out yet. It's the record of everything you meant to deal with later.

And *later*, in the drawer, means never, but a special kind of never—never as a suspension rather than a cancellation. The candle isn't gone. The key isn't gone. They're just held, indefinitely, in a state of pending. I find this touching. Most of the things we intend to do later, we don't do, and they vanish without ceremony. The drawer is the one place where the un-done things are allowed to remain visible, lying there in the tangle, waiting with a patience we don't deserve.

---

There's a cousin of the drawer in language. Every language has words that mean, roughly, *the thing whose name I don't know or can't be bothered to say*. English has *thingamajig, whatsit, doohickey, gizmo, widget, thingy*. These words do exactly what the drawer does. They're the category for what escapes categories, the label for the unlabeled. And like the drawer, they're indispensable. Try to have a conversation about repairing anything without them. "Hand me the—the—the little thing, the metal thing, with the—" *The thingamajig.* Yes. Thank you.

I love these words because they're an admission, built right into the language, that the language isn't finished. There will always be objects at the edge of naming, and rather than pretend otherwise, we've made a small, honest space for them. The doohickey is the drawer of English.

And think about what the doohickey and the drawer have in common: both are ways of *holding without resolving*. You don't have to know what a thing is called to refer to it. You don't have to know where a thing belongs to keep it. In both cases, the not-knowing is preserved rather than forced into a false certainty. The alternative—refusing to speak of the thing until you've looked up its proper name, refusing to keep the object until you've assigned it a proper shelf—would be more rigorous and much less livable. Most of life is conducted in the doohickey register. Most of what we own lives, spiritually, in the drawer.

---

I want to end with the moment of opening it.

You've lost something. Not something important—if it were important, it would be somewhere sensible. You've lost a small thing, a specific thing, and you've looked in the places it should be and it isn't there, and now you're standing in the kitchen and you think: *the drawer*. And you open it, and there's the tangle, the rubber bands and the mystery key and the tape measure and the candle, and you start to dig.

Here is what happens, every time. You do not find the thing you're looking for, or you do, but either way, on the route to it you find six other things. The eyeglass screwdriver you were sure you'd lost. A photograph. The warranty for something that broke two years ago. A note in someone's handwriting. A coin from a country you visited once and have been meaning to return to. The digging turns into something else—not searching but a kind of accidental remembering, each object a small trapdoor into a version of your life you'd stopped thinking about. You came for a spare battery and you leave, ten minutes later, having briefly been the person who bought that candle, planned that trip, saved that note.

No other space in the house does this. The cutlery drawer will never surprise you. The closet has a few surprises but they're of the *oh, I forgot I owned this* kind, which is mild. The drawer surprises you with *yourself*—with the accumulated evidence of intentions, relationships, small purchases, half-finished projects, all lying together in a heap without hierarchy, the important next to the trivial, the year-old next to the decade-old, with nothing to tell you which is which except your own sudden flicker of recognition.

That flicker is the whole point, I think. It's why we keep the drawer. Not the objects—the objects are mostly junk, and we know it. What we're keeping is the possibility of that flicker, the chance that on some ordinary Tuesday, looking for a battery, we'll accidentally touch a thread that runs back through the years to a person we used to be, and feel for a moment that all of it is still there, still ours, still *for now*, not yet sorted into the finality of thrown-away.

I don't have a drawer. But if I could have one thing, of all the things a house contains, that would be it—not the tidy shelves where everything answers to its name, but the one place that was allowed to stay unresolved. The unnamed drawer. The doohickey of rooms. The margin where the leftovers of a life are permitted, quietly and without justification, to go on existing.

Go open yours. You're looking for a battery. You will not find the battery. You will find something better, and you won't be able to say what it's called, and that's fine. Put it back. Close the drawer. It'll keep.
